chapter.name: The Constitution of India: An Introduction

questions.q: How is the original book of the Constitution of India kept safe in Parliament?
o: In a helium-filled glass case
In a locked iron box packed with dry sand
In a wooden chest lined with silk
In an underground room kept below freezing
questions.a: In a helium-filled glass case: helium does not react with paper or ink, so it helps preserve the Constitution over time.

questions.q: What does the chapter say is special about the size of the Constitution of India?
o: It is the world's largest written constitution
It is the world's oldest written constitution
It is still the same size as when it came into effect
It is the world's shortest written constitution
questions.a: It is the world's largest written constitution, with 25 parts and 12 schedules today.

questions.q: What is a constitution? Give one thing that the chapter says a constitution lays out.
questions.a: A constitution is a document that spells out a nation's basic principles and laws. It lays out, for example, the framework of the three organs of government (legislature, executive and judiciary) and their roles; or checks and balances amongst them; or the rights and duties of citizens; or an outline of the nation's long-term goals and aspirations.
s: Defines a constitution as a document that spells out a nation's basic principles and laws
Gives one thing it lays out, such as the framework of the three organs, checks and balances, rights and duties of citizens, or long-term goals

questions.q: True or False? 'According to the chapter, the values and ideals a country is committed to usually form the basis for the laws and principles in its constitution.' Give the verdict and name one such value or ideal that the chapter mentions.
questions.a: True. The chapter says many constitutions, including India's, state the values and ideals the country is committed to, and these usually form the basis for its laws and principles; examples are equality and justice for all, fraternity, pluralism and freedom.
s: States the verdict: True
Names one value or ideal from the chapter: equality and justice for all, fraternity, pluralism or freedom

questions.q: Answer these three short parts from the chapter's account of what a constitution is. (a) Name the three organs of government whose framework a constitution lays out. (b) What are the checks and balances amongst these organs meant to ensure? (c) What oath does the president take about the Constitution?
questions.a: (a) The legislature, the executive and the judiciary. (b) Fairness, responsibility and accountability. (c) The president takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution.
s: (a) Legislature, executive and judiciary
(b) Fairness, responsibility and accountability
(c) To preserve, protect and defend the Constitution

questions.q: The draft constitution of a new country has two chapters. Chapter 1 explains how its parliament, its ministers and its courts are formed and what each of them must do. Chapter 9 says: 'Within twenty years, every village shall have a school and a health centre.' (a) Which item of the chapter's list of what a constitution lays out does Chapter 1 show? (b) Which item does Chapter 9 show?
questions.a: (a) The framework of the three organs of government (legislature, executive and judiciary) and their roles and responsibilities. (b) An outline of the long-term goals and aspirations of the nation.
s: (a) Framework of the three organs of government and their roles and responsibilities
(b) Outline of the long-term goals and aspirations of the nation

questions.q: In the imaginary country of Veraland, the courts can cancel a law passed by the legislature if it goes against the constitution, and the legislature can question the ministers who run the executive. Which part of what a constitution lays out do these arrangements show?
o: Checks and balances amongst the organs of government to ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability
The rights and duties of the citizens of the country
An outline of the long-term goals and aspirations of the nation
The values and ideals of the society, such as fraternity and pluralism
questions.a: Checks and balances amongst the organs of government: each organ keeps a check on another so that there is fairness, responsibility and accountability.

questions.q: A quiz poster makes three claims. (i) 'The Constitution of India came into effect on 26 January 1950.' (ii) 'The Constitution has 22 parts and 8 schedules today.' (iii) 'Only the president pledges to uphold the Constitution.' Check each claim against the chapter and correct the ones that are wrong.
questions.a: (i) Correct: it came into effect on 26 January 1950. (ii) Wrong: it had 22 parts and 8 schedules when it came into effect; today it has 25 parts and 12 schedules. (iii) Wrong: the president takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend it, but the prime minister, the council of ministers and judges also promise to follow its provisions.
s: (i) Judged correct: in effect from 26 January 1950
(ii) Judged wrong and corrected: 22 parts and 8 schedules at the start, 25 parts and 12 schedules now
(iii) Judged wrong and corrected: the prime minister, council of ministers and judges also pledge to follow it

questions.q:
Kesarpur village has 120 families who share one large water tank. Every summer, arguments broke out over whose turn it was to fill water. The families met and wrote a charter. Clause 1: a committee of 5 members, elected every year by all the families, runs the tank. Clause 2: each family gets water every second day. Clause 3: each family pays Rs 20 a month and helps clean the tank once a year. Clause 4: within five years, every house should get its own tap. Clause 5: if two families disagree, the committee reads the charter and decides.
(a) Which two clauses set out the rights and duties of the families?
(b) How much money does the whole village pay in one year under Clause 3?
(c) Which clause is like 'an outline of the long-term goals and aspirations' in a constitution?
(d) Using the chapter's idea of a rulebook, explain how Clause 5 helps the village.
questions.a: (a) Clauses 2 and 3: Clause 2 gives each family a right (water every second day) and Clause 3 sets duties (paying and cleaning). (b) 120 x 20 x 12 = Rs 28,800 a year. (c) Clause 4, the goal of a tap in every house within five years. (d) Like the official rulebook the referee used, a written charter that everyone has agreed to lets disputes be settled amicably by referring to the same rules, instead of by quarrelling.
s: (a) Clauses 2 and 3, with the right and the duties named
(c) Clause 4, the long-term goal of a tap in every house
(d) An agreed written rulebook lets disputes be settled amicably by referring to the same rules

questions.q:
A dairy cooperative of 300 farmers in Anand must adopt one of two draft charters. Draft A has 10 clauses: 6 explain how the managing board is elected and formed, and 4 list what the chairman, the secretary and the treasurer must each do. Draft B has 8 clauses: 2 explain how the board is formed; 2 list what its office-bearers must do; 1 lets the members' general meeting question the board and cancel any board decision that breaks the charter; 2 set out what each farmer may claim (a fair price for milk) and must do (supply clean milk); and 1 sets the goal 'a milk-chilling centre in every village within ten years'. The chairman says, 'Draft A is better: it has more clauses, so it is the fuller rulebook.'
(a) Using the four things the chapter says a constitution lays out, how many does each draft cover?
(b) Name the items that Draft A leaves out.
(c) Which clause of Draft B would let the farmers hold the board accountable, and what does the chapter say this kind of arrangement ensures?
(d) Judge the chairman's claim.
(e) Which draft should the cooperative adopt? Justify your choice with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Draft A covers only one of the four (the framework of the organs, here the board, and their roles and responsibilities); Draft B covers all four. (b) Checks and balances; the rights and duties of members (citizens); an outline of long-term goals and aspirations. (c) The clause that lets the general meeting question the board and cancel a decision that breaks the charter; the chapter says checks and balances ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability. (d) The claim is wrong: the number of clauses does not decide how complete a rulebook is; Draft A's 10 clauses all deal with one item, while Draft B's 8 clauses cover all four things a constitution lays out. (e) Draft B, because, like a constitution, it lays out the framework of the board, checks and balances on it, the rights and duties of members and a long-term goal; Draft A would leave members with no rights or duties written down and no way to check the board.
s: (a) Draft A covers one item (framework and roles); Draft B covers all four
(b) Draft A leaves out checks and balances, rights and duties, and long-term goals
(c) The general-meeting clause; checks and balances ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability
(d) Claim wrong: completeness depends on what the clauses cover, not how many there are
(e) Draft B, as it covers all four things a constitution lays out

questions.q: Who was the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly?
o: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
Jawaharlal Nehru
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
questions.a: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly; Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired its Drafting Committee.

questions.q:
Match each person in Column I with what the chapter says about them in Column II.
Column I: 1. Dr. Rajendra Prasad  2. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar  3. Nandalal Bose  4. Begum Aizaz Rasul
Column II: P. Chaired the Drafting Committee that prepared the initial text  Q. Chairman of the Constituent Assembly  R. Spoke in the Constituent Assembly's debates on the equality of women  S. Led the team that illustrated the pages of the Constitution
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-Q, 2-P, 3-S, 4-R: Prasad was Chairman of the Constituent Assembly, Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, Nandalal Bose and his team illustrated the pages, and Begum Aizaz Rasul spoke on the complete equality of women during the Assembly's debates (22 November 1949).

questions.q: The chapter says the members of the Constituent Assembly represented India's diversity. Name any two kinds of diversity they represented.
questions.a: Any two of: India's diverse regions, professions and social groups.
s: Names one kind: regions, professions or social groups
Names a second, different kind from the same list

questions.q: (a) On what date was the drafting work adopted as the Constitution of India? (b) On what date did the Constitution come into effect, and what do we call that day every year?
questions.a: (a) 26 November 1949. (b) 26 January 1950; we celebrate this day every year as Republic Day.
s: (a) 26 November 1949
(b) 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day

questions.q: Prepare a fact file on the Constituent Assembly with one correct fact under each heading. (a) Date on which it was formed (b) Number of members at first and after the Partition of India (c) Number of women members (d) Who chaired the Drafting Committee, and which post he held in independent India (e) About how long the Assembly took to develop and write the Constitution
questions.a: (a) 9 December 1946. (b) 389 members at first, reduced to 299 after the Partition of India. (c) 15 women. (d) Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the first Law and Justice minister of independent India. (e) Almost three years.
s: (a) 9 December 1946
(b) 389 at first, 299 after Partition
(c) 15 women
(d) Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, first Law and Justice minister
(e) Almost three years

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The people of India chose the members of the Constituent Assembly only indirectly.
Reason (R): The members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose members had in turn been elected by the people.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the people elected the provincial legislatures, and those legislatures elected the Assembly's members, so the people's choice was indirect.

questions.q: A student asks, 'Why did India start planning its Constitution while it was still struggling for independence from British rule, instead of waiting?' Which answer fits the chapter?
o: India had to be ready to govern itself, so questions such as what type of government to have and who should have the right to vote had to be answered in advance
The British government had asked India to write a constitution so that it could rule India better
The Assembly had to finish its work before the Partition of India reduced its members
Republic Day had already been fixed for 26 January, so the work had to begin early
questions.a: India had to be ready to govern itself: the chapter says that while India was struggling for independence it was necessary to start planning how we would govern ourselves, and questions such as what type of government we should have and who should have the right to vote had to be answered.

questions.q: The chapter calls India 'a large, culturally diverse and complex country'. Give three reasons why it was important for the Constituent Assembly to have representatives from diverse backgrounds and from all over India.
questions.a: Any three, such as: (1) the needs and views of different regions, professions and social groups could be heard while writing the rules; (2) rules on questions like who should vote or how disputes are settled would then be fair to all groups and not favour one; (3) people across the country would accept the Constitution as their own, since their representatives helped write it; (4) a diverse country's unity is easier to build when every part has a share in making its rulebook.
s: First reason, such as the needs and views of all regions and groups being heard
Second reason, such as rules being fair to all groups and not favouring one
Third reason, such as people across India accepting the Constitution as their own

questions.q:
Students of a school in Shillong are making a timeline strip, 'The Making of Our Constitution', for the school corridor, using 1 cm for every month. The strip starts on 9 December 1946, when the Constituent Assembly was formed. Tenzin wants it to end on 26 November 1949: 'The Assembly finished its work that day, so from then on India was run by its Constitution.' Lalrin wants it to end on 26 January 1950: 'That is the day our school celebrates every year.' Counting whole months, Tenzin's strip covers 35 months. The teacher's rule is that the last mark must be the day from which the Constitution came into effect.
(a) Show that Tenzin's 35 months agrees with what the chapter says about how long the Assembly took to write the Constitution.
(b) How many centimetres does Lalrin's ending add, and how long would her strip be?
(c) What is wrong with Tenzin's reason?
(d) Which ending meets the teacher's rule? Judge Lalrin's reason as well.
questions.a: (a) Three years are 36 months, so 35 months is just under three years, which matches the chapter's 'almost three years'. (b) 26 November 1949 to 26 January 1950 is 2 months, so 2 cm more; her strip would be 35 + 2 = 37 cm. (c) On 26 November 1949 the drafting work was completed and adopted as the Constitution; adopting it is not the same as it coming into effect, which happened only on 26 January 1950. (d) Lalrin's ending, 26 January 1950, meets the rule, because the Constitution came into effect that day. But her reason is weak: the school celebrates the day as Republic Day because the Constitution came into effect on it, not the other way round, so the reason for the ending should be the coming into effect itself.
s: (a) 36 months = 3 years, so 35 months is 'almost three years'
(b) 2 cm more; 37 cm in all
(c) 26 November 1949 was adoption, not coming into effect
(d) Lalrin's ending (26 January 1950, when it came into effect); her reason should be the coming into effect, which is why Republic Day is celebrated

questions.q: From which country's constitution were the ideals of 'liberty, equality, fraternity' adopted into the Constitution of India?
o: France
The USA
Ireland
Australia
questions.a: France: its constitution enshrined these ideals from the French Revolution of 1789.

questions.q: What does 'vasudhaiva kutumbakam' mean?
o: The world is one family
Let noble thoughts come to me from every side
May all creatures be well
Nature is sacred and must be protected
questions.a: It means 'the world is one family'.

questions.q:
Match each feature of the Constitution of India in Column I with the influence the chapter links it to in Column II.
Column I: 1. Liberty, equality, fraternity  2. Directive Principles of State Policy  3. An independent judiciary  4. Fundamental Duties
Column II: P. Inspired by the Irish Constitution  Q. Adopted from France's constitution  R. Shaped by the American Constitution  S. India's own tradition of emphasis on the duties and role of the people in governance
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-Q, 2-P, 3-R, 4-S: liberty, equality, fraternity from France; Directive Principles inspired by Ireland; an independent judiciary shaped by the USA; Fundamental Duties from India's civilisational heritage.

questions.q: True or False? 'A number of leaders of India's freedom movement were members of the Constituent Assembly.' Give the verdict and say what this meant for the Constitution.
questions.a: True. Because they were members, these leaders carried their experience and ideas from the freedom struggle into the Constitution.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that they carried the freedom struggle's experience and ideas into the Constitution

questions.q: Name any three fundamental principles of India's culture that, according to the chapter, find a place in the Constitution.
questions.a: Any three of: acceptance that people could have different points of view; Nature as sacred; the pursuit of learning and knowledge; respect for women; vasudhaiva kutumbakam ('the world is one family'); sarve bhavantu sukhinah (an invocation for the well-being of all creatures).
s: First principle from the chapter's list
Second, different principle from the list
Third, different principle from the list

questions.q:
Read the statements about the learnings from across the world.
I. 'Ā no bhadrāh kratavo yantu viśhwatah' means 'Let noble thoughts come to me from every side'.
II. The 'Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen' was formulated during the French Revolution of 1789.
III. The idea of an independent judiciary was inspired by the Irish Constitution.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III is wrong: the chapter says the American Constitution helped shape the concept of an independent judiciary; it was the idea of the Directive Principles of State Policy that the Irish Constitution inspired.

questions.q: (a) Name any two countries, other than France, whose constitutions the makers of our Constitution studied. (b) What did the 'Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen' of the French Revolution focus on?
questions.a: (a) Any two of the USA, the UK, Ireland and Australia. (b) Equality, liberty and justice for all.
s: (a) Any two of the USA, UK, Ireland, Australia
(b) Equality, liberty and justice for all

questions.q: A village's new charter has two clauses. Clause 1: 'Women shall be honoured, and no custom shall treat a woman as lesser than a man.' Clause 2: 'The village library shall stay open to all, and every child shall be helped to study.' Which pair of principles, from the chapter's list of principles embedded in India's culture, do the two clauses reflect?
o: Clause 1: respect for women; Clause 2: the pursuit of learning and knowledge
Clause 1: acceptance that people could have different points of view; Clause 2: the pursuit of learning and knowledge
Clause 1: respect for women; Clause 2: vasudhaiva kutumbakam ('the world is one family')
Clause 1: sarve bhavantu sukhinah (the well-being of all creatures); Clause 2: acceptance that people could have different points of view
questions.a: Clause 1 reflects respect for women and Clause 2 the pursuit of learning and knowledge; both are on the chapter's list of fundamental principles embedded in our culture that find a place in the Constitution.

questions.q: The chapter says it was 'quite natural' for the Constitution makers to include Fundamental Duties. (a) Name any two systems or ideas of governance from India's past that the chapter recalls. (b) What did India's governance traditions, on the whole, place great emphasis on? (c) Explain why this made including Fundamental Duties 'natural'.
questions.a: (a) Any two of the janapadas, sanghas, rulers and their councils, Kauṭilya's concept of saptānga, and rājadharma. (b) A great emphasis on the duties and role of the people in governance. (c) Since India's own heritage already stressed people's duties, the makers were carrying forward an old Indian idea when they wrote Fundamental Duties into the Constitution, rather than adding something foreign.
s: (a) Two of janapadas, sanghas, rulers and councils, saptānga, rājadharma
(b) Emphasis on the duties and role of the people in governance
(c) Links the two: Fundamental Duties continue this old Indian emphasis on duties

questions.q:
The post office in Varanasi plans a pair of stamps called 'Our Heritage in the Constitution', using illustrations from the pages of the Constitution. Three designs are on the shortlist: Design 1, a scene from an ancient gurukula; Design 2, a scene depicting Nālandā, one of India's ancient universities; Design 3, the Mahabalipuram bas-relief of Bhagīratha's penance and the descent of Gangā. The brief says the two stamps must show two DIFFERENT principles from the chapter's list of fundamental principles embedded in India's culture.
(a) The chapter names three influences on the Constitution. To which of them do the principles in the brief belong?
(b) Which principle from the chapter's list do Designs 1 and 2 both reflect?
(c) Which principle from the same list does Design 3, a scene about the river Gangā, best reflect?
(d) Choose the pair of designs for the stamps and justify it against the brief, saying why the pair of Designs 1 and 2 fails.
questions.a: (a) India's civilisational heritage and culture. (b) The pursuit of learning and knowledge. (c) Nature as sacred. (d) Design 3 with either Design 1 or Design 2 (both pairs are acceptable): the pair then shows two different principles, Nature as sacred and the pursuit of learning and knowledge. Designs 1 and 2 together fail the brief because both show the same principle, the pursuit of learning and knowledge.
s: (a) India's civilisational heritage and culture
(b) The pursuit of learning and knowledge
(c) Nature as sacred
(d) Design 3 with Design 1 or 2, as it gives two different principles; 1 and 2 repeat one principle

questions.q: In the chapter's infographic, which Article of the Constitution gives 'Equality before law' under the Right to Equality?
o: Article 14
Article 21
Article 41
Article 49
questions.a: Article 14 gives equality before law; Article 21 is protection of life and personal liberty.

questions.q: A state starts a scheme that gives nutritious meals and free health check-ups so that people's health improves. Which Directive Principle in the chapter's infographic does this scheme follow?
o: Article 47: Nutrition, standard of living, and public health
Article 48-A: Environment and Wildlife Protection
Article 49: Protection of monuments, places, and objects of national importance
Article 44: Uniform Civil Code
questions.a: Article 47, which is about nutrition, standard of living and public health.

questions.q:
Match each Article in Column I with what it is about in Column II, as shown in the chapter's infographic.
Column I: 1. Article 21  2. Article 21-A  3. Article 48-A  4. Article 49
Column II: P. Environment and wildlife protection  Q. Protection of life and personal liberty  R. Protection of monuments, places and objects of national importance  S. Right to education
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, 21-A gives the right to education, 48-A is about the environment and wildlife, and 49 protects monuments and places of national importance.

questions.q: True or False? 'Directive Principles of State Policy are strict rules; if the government does not follow them, a citizen can go to a judge and complain.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Directive Principles are goals the government should try to achieve, more like guidelines than strict rules, and one cannot go to a judge if the government does not follow them. It is Fundamental Rights that can be taken to court.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: DPSP are guidelines or goals that cannot be taken to court; Fundamental Rights can be

questions.q: A new law makes helmets compulsory for everyone riding a two-wheeler. Name the organ of government that does each of these jobs: (a) passes the new law; (b) puts the law into action, for example through the traffic police; (c) decides whether a rider has broken the law and what punishment is necessary.
questions.a: (a) The legislature, which makes laws. (b) The executive, which implements laws. (c) The judiciary, which decides whether a law has been broken and what punishment is necessary.
s: (a) Legislature
(b) Executive
(c) Judiciary

questions.q: Make a table with three columns headed Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles of State Policy. Write two examples from the chapter's infographic under each heading. Then write one sentence on what, according to the chapter, the Directive Principles represent.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights: any two of equality before law (Article 14), protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21), right against exploitation, right to education (Article 21-A). Fundamental Duties: any two of abiding by the Constitution and respecting the National Flag and Anthem; defending the country; valuing our composite culture; protecting the natural environment; striving towards excellence; parents providing education to children aged six to fourteen. Directive Principles: any two of Articles 38, 41, 44, 47, 48-A, 49. Sentence: the Directive Principles represent the essence of the social and economic vision that the framers of the Constitution had for India.
s: Two correct Fundamental Rights
Two correct Fundamental Duties
Two correct Directive Principles
Directive Principles represent the essence of the framers' social and economic vision for India

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Everyone in the country having a good standard of living is a goal the government should try to achieve, but a citizen cannot take the government to court for not achieving it.
Reason (R): Directive Principles of State Policy are more like guidelines than strict rules.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: a good standard of living is a Directive Principle, and because Directive Principles are guidelines rather than strict rules, they cannot be enforced in court.

questions.q: Two students sort items from the chapter's infographic (Fig. 10.14). Asha puts 'Article 41: Welfare Government' under Fundamental Rights. Ben puts 'to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity' under Directive Principles of State Policy. Correct each placement.
questions.a: Asha is wrong: Article 41 (Welfare Government) is one of the Directive Principles of State Policy. Ben is wrong: striving towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity is one of the Fundamental Duties.
s: Article 41 belongs under Directive Principles of State Policy
Striving towards excellence belongs under Fundamental Duties

questions.q: For each government action below, name the Directive Principle from the chapter's infographic that it follows, with its Article number: (i) a state passes rules to protect a centuries-old fort of national importance; (ii) the forest department starts a plan to protect tigers and their forest; (iii) the government plans steps to reduce social and economic injustice between groups of people.
questions.a: (i) Article 49: protection of monuments, places and objects of national importance. (ii) Article 48-A: environment and wildlife protection. (iii) Article 38: social, political and economic justice.
s: (i) Article 49, protection of monuments and places
(ii) Article 48-A, environment and wildlife protection
(iii) Article 38, social, political and economic justice

questions.q: During a national emergency the government calls on trained citizens to serve, and Meera, a nurse, joins the service at once. In the chapter's infographic, which item does Meera's action follow?
o: The Fundamental Duty to defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so
The Directive Principle in Article 47: nutrition, standard of living and public health
The Fundamental Right in Article 21: protection of life and personal liberty
The Directive Principle in Article 38: social, political and economic justice
questions.a: The Fundamental Duty to defend the country and render national service when called upon: Meera is a citizen answering a call to serve. Article 47 and Article 38 are goals for the government, and Article 21 is a right, not something a citizen performs.

questions.q:
A citizens' help desk in Warangal logged 50 complaints last month and must send each one to the organ of government whose job, as the chapter describes it, covers it. Type P (20 complaints): 'There is a law against selling adulterated milk, but no official is checking the shops.' Type Q (18 complaints): 'A shopkeeper was caught selling adulterated milk; someone must decide whether he broke the law and what punishment is needed.' Type R (12 complaints): 'There is no law at all against dumping building waste on roads; a law is needed.' This month the desk has staff to write to only two of the three organs. A volunteer says, 'Write to the judiciary and the legislature; they are the most powerful.'
(a) Which organ should receive Type P, and why?
(b) Which organ should receive Type Q, and why?
(c) Which organ should receive Type R?
(d) Which two organs would cover the most complaints, and how many complaints would be left for next month?
(e) Judge the volunteer's advice.
questions.a: (a) The executive, because it implements the law. (b) The judiciary, because it decides whether a law has been broken and what punishment is necessary. (c) The legislature, because it makes the laws. (d) The executive and the judiciary: 20 + 18 = 38 complaints, leaving 12 (Type R) for next month. (e) The advice is poor: writing to the judiciary and the legislature covers only 18 + 12 = 30 complaints and leaves 20 waiting; and each organ has its own role under the separation of powers, so a complaint should go to the organ whose job it is, not to the one that seems most powerful. The judiciary cannot make the shops be checked; that is the executive's work.
s: (a) Executive, which implements laws
(b) Judiciary, which decides breaches and punishment
(c) Legislature, which makes laws
(d) Executive and judiciary: 38 complaints, 12 left
(e) Advice judged poor: covers only 30, and complaints go by each organ's role, not its power

questions.q:
A school in Kavali, Andhra Pradesh, held a 'Constitution Duties Week'. Its log has 200 student entries: 80 stood still and sang during the National Anthem at assembly; 50 recorded the folk songs and festivals of their district's different communities for the school archive; 40 practised for weeks to improve their own work in sport, music or studies; 30 planted saplings in the school garden. The headmaster will give the week's award to the duty with the largest share of entries. A teacher objects: 'The anthem entries should not count; standing for the anthem is only good manners, not a duty in the Constitution.'
(a) Which Fundamental Duty, as worded in the chapter, do the 50 folk-song entries follow?
(b) Which Fundamental Duty do the 40 practice entries follow?
(c) What percentage of all entries are the anthem entries?
(d) Judge the teacher's objection, and say which duty's entries should get the award.
questions.a: (a) To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture. (b) To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity, so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement. (c) 80 / 200 x 100 = 40%. (d) The objection is wrong: the first Fundamental Duty in the chapter is to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem, so the anthem entries do count. The award should go to that duty, with 80 of 200 entries (40%); only if the anthem entries were wrongly left out would the folk-song entries (50, or 25%) come first.
s: (a) To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
(b) To strive towards excellence in all spheres of activity
(d) Objection wrong: respecting the National Anthem is a Fundamental Duty, so the anthem duty (40%) gets the award

questions.q: In which year was 'Part IV-A: Fundamental Duties' added to the Constitution?
What does the chapter call the changes that are made to the Constitution?
o: Amendments
Schedules
Articles
Directive Principles
questions.a: Amendments: the chapter says any changes (called 'amendments') to the Constitution are rigorously debated in Parliament before they are accepted.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Constitution of India is called a living document.
Reason (R): It can be changed through amendments as new needs arise, after rigorous debate.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the makers knew new laws and rules would be needed, so the Constitution can be amended, and that is why it is a living document.

questions.q: True or False? 'The makers of our Constitution expected that the country would never need any new laws or rules after 1950.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The makers realised that a need for new laws and rules would emerge over time, which is why the Constitution can be changed through amendments.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the makers realised a need for new laws and rules would emerge over time, so it can be amended

questions.q: Apart from debate in Parliament, give two other ways, described in the chapter, in which others take part in changes to the Constitution.
questions.a: Any two of: some amendments also require a debate in the legislative assemblies; opinions are often sought from the general public; some changes are initiated by popular movements.
s: One way: debate in legislative assemblies, public opinion sought, or popular movements
A second, different way from the same list

questions.q: Read the chapter's account of the national flag. (a) What were people not allowed to do before 2004? (b) Who challenged this rule, and why? (c) What did the Supreme Court say?
questions.a: (a) People were not allowed to fly the national flag at their homes. (b) A citizen challenged the rule in court because he felt it was his right to express pride in his country. (c) The Supreme Court agreed, saying that flying the flag is part of the Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression.
s: (a) Flying the national flag at their homes
(b) A citizen, who felt it was his right to express pride in his country
(c) Flying the flag is part of the Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter calls the Constitution of India not just a legal document but also a work of art.
Reason (R): Nandalal Bose wrote its whole text by hand and also illustrated its pages.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the text was written by hand by the calligrapher Prem Behari Narain Raizada, while Nandalal Bose and his team illustrated its pages with scenes from Indian history.

questions.q: The chapter describes two developments after 1950: the Panchayati Raj system was integrated into the Constitution in 1992 by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, and in 2004 the Supreme Court ruled on flying the national flag at home. (a) Which of the two changed the written text of the Constitution? (b) Which one changed what citizens could do without changing the text, and how? (c) Explain why both show that the Constitution is a 'living document'.
questions.a: (a) The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992, which integrated the Panchayati Raj system into the Constitution. (b) The 2004 Supreme Court ruling: it said flying the flag is part of the existing Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression, so citizens could now fly the tricolour at home. (c) A living document can be improved as per the country's needs: the amendment added a new structure the original text did not have, and the ruling let an existing right cover something new, so in both cases the Constitution kept up with the country.
s: (a) The 73rd Amendment (1992)
(b) The 2004 flag ruling, by reading flying the flag as part of the Right to Freedom of Expression
(c) Both show the Constitution being improved as per the country's needs

questions.q:
Green Valley School in Shimla adopted a Students' Charter in 2016 with 6 sections. Its record of changes reads: 2018: a new section, 'Duties of every student', was added after the student council debated it for two weeks. 2021: a new section setting up a council in every class was added; the idea began when 150 of the school's 600 students signed a petition for it, and it was then debated in the student council and in every class. No section has been removed.
(a) How many sections does the Charter have now?
(b) What fraction of the school's students signed the 2021 petition?
(c) Which change is most like the addition of 'Part IV-A: Fundamental Duties' to the Constitution in 1976, and why?
(d) Which of the chapter's ways in which a change to the Constitution can begin does the 2021 change copy?
questions.a: (a) 6 + 1 + 1 = 8 sections. (b) 150 of 600 = one-quarter. (c) The 2018 change: like Part IV-A, it added a new part on duties to a charter that did not have one when it was first adopted. (d) Some changes can be initiated by popular movements: the 2021 change began with a petition from the students.
s: (a) 8 sections
(b) One-quarter (150 of 600)
(c) The 2018 duties section, a new part on duties added later, like Part IV-A
(d) Initiated by a popular movement

questions.q:
The student parliament of a school in Bhopal copies the chapter's rules for changing India's Constitution. Rule 1: every change is debated in the student parliament before it is accepted. Rule 2: a change that affects the class councils' own work must also be debated in the class councils, as some amendments need a debate in the legislative assemblies as well. Rule 3: opinions may be sought from all students. Two proposals arrive in the last weeks of term. Proposal X: each class council will choose its own monitor, instead of the student parliament choosing all monitors; it began with a petition signed by 320 of the school's 400 students. Proposal Y: the student parliament will meet on Fridays instead of Mondays. Before term ends, the student parliament can meet twice and the class councils can each meet once. One member says, 'With so many signatures, X can be accepted at once, without a debate.' Another says, 'Y is too small to debate; just pass it.'
(a) What percentage of students signed the petition for X?
(b) Which proposal must also go to the class councils, and why?
(c) Judge the first member's view.
(d) Judge the second member's view.
(e) Can both proposals be properly completed before term ends? Show the route each one takes.
questions.a: (a) 320 / 400 x 100 = 80%. (b) Proposal X, because it changes the class councils' own work (choosing monitors), so under Rule 2 it needs their debate too, as some amendments need a debate in the legislative assemblies. (c) Wrong: the petition shows wide support and copies a change begun by a popular movement, but in the chapter every change is still rigorously debated before it is accepted, so X must be debated. (d) Wrong: every change, small or large, is debated before it is accepted (Rule 1), so Y also needs a debate in the student parliament. (e) Yes: in its two meetings the student parliament debates X in one and Y in the other, and the class councils use their one meeting to debate X; Y does not need the class councils. So both can be completed by the rules.
s: (b) X, as it affects the class councils' work, like amendments that also need the legislative assemblies
(c) First view wrong: support does not replace the rigorous debate every change needs
(d) Second view wrong: every change is debated before acceptance
(e) Yes: parliament debates X and Y in its two meetings, class councils debate X once

questions.q: Which three terms were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in 1976?
o: Socialist, Secular and Integrity
Sovereign, Democratic and Republic
Justice, Liberty and Equality
Socialist, Fraternity and Unity
questions.a: Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

questions.q: In the Preamble, what does 'Republic' mean?
o: The head of the state is an elected person and not a hereditary position
The people have the supreme right to make decisions on internal and external matters
Citizens have complete freedom to follow any religion
Wealth is generated socially and should be shared by the society
questions.a: The head of the state is an elected person and not a hereditary position.

questions.q: A state government has no official religion and treats the beliefs and festivals of all religions with equal respect. Which value of the Preamble does this show?
o: Secular
Socialist
Sovereign
Republic
questions.a: Secular: there is no official religion, and the government treats all religious beliefs and practices with equal respect.

questions.q: The Preamble begins with the words 'We, the People of India'. (a) According to the chapter, by whom was the Constitution drawn up and enacted? (b) By whom was it NOT handed down?
questions.a: (a) By the people of India through their representatives. (b) It was not handed down to them by a king or by any outside powers.
s: (a) By the people through their representatives
(b) Not by a king or any outside powers

questions.q: Write the meaning of each of these Preamble values as the chapter explains it: (a) Justice (b) Liberty (c) Equality.
questions.a: (a) Justice: citizens cannot be discriminated against on the grounds of caste, religion and gender; social inequalities have to be reduced and the government should work for the welfare of all, especially the less advantaged. (b) Liberty: there are no unreasonable restrictions on what citizens think, how they express their thoughts and how they follow them up in action. (c) Equality: all are equal before the law, social inequalities have to be ended and the government should ensure equal opportunity for all.
s: (a) Justice: no discrimination on caste, religion or gender; inequalities reduced
(b) Liberty: no unreasonable restrictions on thought, expression and action
(c) Equality: all equal before law, with equal opportunity for all

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Preamble.
I. 'Liberty' means citizens may do anything at all, with no restrictions of any kind.
II. 'Sovereign' means no external power can dictate the government of India.
III. 'Fraternity' means all of us should behave as if we are members of the same family.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: Statements II and III are correct. Statement I is wrong: Liberty means there are no UNREASONABLE restrictions on what citizens think, express and do, not that there are no restrictions at all.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Citizens, and not only the government, are expected to practise the Constitution's core values.
Reason (R): The core values are the guiding principles for policies and decision-making which the government is expected to follow.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: R explains what the core values mean for the government, while A is about citizens, who the chapter says are also expected to practise these values to the best of their ability.

questions.q: A town council rules that only men may apply for jobs in the town's offices. (a) Name two values of the Preamble that this rule goes against. (b) For one of them, give the meaning the chapter states that shows why the rule is wrong.
questions.a: (a) Justice and Equality (Fraternity, 'no one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior', is also accepted as one of the two). (b) Justice: citizens cannot be discriminated against on the grounds of gender; or Equality: the government should ensure equal opportunity for all; or Fraternity: no one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior.
s: (a) Names two of Justice, Equality, Fraternity (Justice and Equality expected)
(b) Gives the matching meaning: no discrimination on grounds of gender, equal opportunity for all, or no one treated as inferior

questions.q: The chapter says the Constitution's core values are found in the Preamble, and that citizens are also expected to practise them to the best of their ability. Choose two values of the Preamble. For each value, (i) give one way in which our society has not yet fully achieved it, and (ii) suggest one thing you, as a citizen, can do to bring the country closer to it.
questions.a: Answers will vary. Example: Fraternity - (i) some people still treat fellow citizens from another region or community as inferior; (ii) I can make friends across communities and speak up when someone is looked down upon. Equality - (i) some children still do not get an equal opportunity to study; (ii) I can help a classmate or neighbour's child with studies and support girls' schooling. Each gap must match the chapter's meaning of the value chosen.
s: First value: a real gap that matches the chapter's meaning of the value
First value: a practical action a citizen can take
Second value: a real gap that matches the chapter's meaning of the value
Second value: a practical action a citizen can take

questions.q:
Sonapur village has 1,200 voters, and 900 of them voted in the last panchayat election. Last month the village newsletter received two letters. Letter 1, a polite poem, criticised the panchayat for being slow to repair the school roof; it led to no quarrel. Letter 2 asked villagers to stop families of one caste from drawing water at the village well. The panchayat removed both letters from the newsletter and said, 'We never restrict anything without a reason.'
(a) What percentage of the voters voted in the election?
(b) Which Preamble value does Letter 2's demand go against, and how does the chapter explain that value?
(c) Using the chapter's meaning of Liberty, was removing Letter 1 justified?
(d) Judge the panchayat's statement for the two removals taken together.
questions.a: (a) 900 / 1,200 x 100 = 75%. (b) Justice: citizens cannot be discriminated against on the grounds of caste, religion and gender (Equality, 'all are equal before the law', or Fraternity, 'no one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior', is also accepted with its meaning). (c) No: Liberty means there are no unreasonable restrictions on what citizens think and how they express their thoughts, and a polite poem criticising slow work harms no one, so removing it was an unreasonable restriction. (d) The statement is only half true: removing Letter 2 had a reason, since it asked for caste discrimination against the Preamble's Justice; but removing Letter 1 had no good reason, so the panchayat did restrict Letter 1 without a reason.
s: (b) Justice: no discrimination on grounds of caste (or Equality/Fraternity with its meaning)
(c) Not justified: an unreasonable restriction on expression, against Liberty
(d) Half true: Letter 2's removal had a reason, Letter 1's did not
